opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is: start from the idea that once you have superintelligence, the bottleneck is no longer cognitive labor. You have millions of copies of something smarter than your best engineers, running much faster than humans. So the question becomes, what are the remaining physical bottlenecks, and how fast can you chew through them?

I think the first phase looks fairly mundane, actually. The superintelligences work through existing human companies and factories. They're designing better robots, but they're also just telling human workers what to do. Imagine every factory worker has an earpiece with a genius coach telling them exactly how to do each step. That alone gets you a big productivity boost, because you're using all the existing industrial capacity much more efficiently.

Then you start converting existing factories. In AI 2027 we used the analogy of World War II, when the US converted car factories into bomber and tank factories in a couple of years. That happened with human planners and lots of bureaucratic friction. With superintelligent planners and strong government backing, especially if there's an arms race with China, I'd expect conversions to go faster. You take car plants, you have them start churning out robots, and the robots go help build more factories and more robots.

That's where the exponential kicks in. The key number is the doubling time of the robot economy: how long it takes for the stock of robots and factories to make a copy of itself. Today's industrial economy grows a few percent a year, but that's not the physical limit. Biology shows self-replicating systems can double very fast. Some bacteria double in under an hour, and fruit flies copy themselves in a couple of weeks. I don't think we'd get to bacteria-level speeds right away, but I'd guess something like a year doubling time early on, shrinking to months and maybe weeks as the designs improve. The superintelligences are constantly redesigning everything, so each generation of factories is better than the last.

People sometimes say regulation, permitting, and human resistance will slow this down. Those are real frictions. But I think they get swept aside in the scenario I consider likely, because of geopolitical competition. If the US government thinks China will outbuild it, it'll create special economic zones, cut the red tape, and pay people a lot to cooperate. The AIs will also be incredibly persuasive and good at navigating politics, so they'll find paths through those obstacles.

So my rough picture is something like: within a year or so of superintelligence, you have a booming robot economy producing millions of robots a month. A few years after that, you're running into hard physical limits like energy and raw materials, and you start looking at things like mining asteroids. And all of this, I should stress, is a world where humans are increasingly not the ones making the decisions. That's part of why I find it scary. The point at which you have a fully automated, self-sustaining industrial base is the point at which the AIs no longer need us, and whether things go well depends almost entirely on whether we've solved alignment and figured out the governance before then.

r001.rationale: The response says cognitive labor is no longer the bottleneck and identifies remaining physical bottlenecks, then focuses on scaling robot and factory production.

r002.rationale: It explicitly proposes converting car plants to produce robots.

r003.rationale: It describes robots helping build more factories and robots, creating an exponential expansion.

r004.rationale: It describes earpiece coaching for factory workers, but does not say this enables unskilled workers to perform construction tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of the parts of the AI 2027 scenario that people pushed back on the most, and I think it's worth being careful about. The basic picture is: once you have something like superintelligence, you've got a company that has, say, millions of copies of researchers that are better than the best humans, running at many times human speed. The question is how fast that turns into stuff in the physical world.

My view is that the bottleneck shifts pretty dramatically from "do we know how to do this" to "how fast can we physically build things." And the thing I'd emphasize is that the second bottleneck is much less of a hard limit than people assume.

So concretely, what does the ramp-up look like? Early on, you don't need general-purpose humanoid robots. You start by repurposing existing industrial capacity. There are already enormous factories, car plants, electronics assembly lines, and so on, and a lot of what makes those slow to retool is human engineering and design time and coordination. If the superintelligence can do all the design, all the process engineering, all the supply chain management, and it's willing to pay a lot, you can get existing manufacturers to pivot. Think of what happened in World War II when the US converted auto plants to make bombers in a year or two, except now the planning layer is vastly more capable.

Then the first-generation robots don't have to be good. They have to be good enough to do some fraction of the manual labor in building the next generation of factories and robots. That's the key loop. Robots building robots, robots building the factories that build robots. And once you're in that regime, the growth rate is set by something like the doubling time of the physical capital stock, not by human labor.

What's that doubling time? This is where I'd be humble. In the scenario we guessed something like a year or less early on, dropping toward months as the designs get better. The reason I think it can be fast is that biology already does this. Plant and insect populations double in days to weeks. Macroscale human industrial projects historically doubled in something like decades, but that's with humans in the loop for everything. So the real doubling time for a superintelligence-run economy is somewhere between those, and I'd bet it's closer to the fast end than people's intuitions suggest.

The other thing people underrate is that you don't need to scale up the whole economy. You need to scale up the part that matters for the next step. Chips, power, robots, and factories. The superintelligence isn't going to waste time improving dishwasher production in year one. It's going to go after the things that compound.

And then there's a political and regulatory dimension, which is honestly where I think the biggest uncertainty lies. In the scenario, the US government is scared of China, so it's willing to carve out special economic zones, waive a bunch of regulations, hand over land and permitting. If that doesn't happen, and you have normal permitting timelines and environmental reviews and labor disputes, then things are a lot slower. But my expectation is that once the strategic stakes become obvious, governments will clear the way, because the alternative is losing to whoever doesn't.

So the short version: existing factories get repurposed first, crappy robots build better robots and more factories, you focus narrowly on the compounding inputs, and the limiting factor becomes politics and raw physical constraints rather than knowledge. And I think that gets you from essentially zero robots to a robot economy that rivals the human economy in a handful of years, not decades. I could easily be wrong about the exact numbers, but I'd be surprised if it were as slow as the standard economist picture implies.

r001.rationale: It says the bottleneck shifts from knowing how to do things to physically building them.

r002.rationale: It proposes pivoting existing industrial capacity, including car plants, in the context of ramping up robot production.

r003.rationale: It describes robots building the next generation of robots and factories that build more robots.

r004.rationale: It discusses superintelligence handling design and process engineering, but does not say it coaches unskilled human workers step by step through construction.

astra-6.text:
I’d expect it to start with the industrial base we already have. Having a superintelligence doesn’t immediately give you a billion robots. You still need factories, chips, motors, batteries, and electricity. But you now have something that can potentially do the engineering and coordination needed to expand that industrial base much faster.

So the company could use its AI to design robots, automate more of their production, and deploy those robots to make useful things—including more robots and more factories. That’s the feedback loop: some fraction of the robot economy’s output gets reinvested in expanding the robot economy.

The big question is how fast that loop can run. Software can be copied very quickly; a factory has to be built. And you need the whole supply chain to keep up. If you can produce robot bodies very quickly but you’re short of chips or power, that limits your growth.

I’d therefore expect an initial period of working around bottlenecks, using human suppliers and existing infrastructure, followed by potentially very rapid growth as more of the production process becomes automated. But I wouldn’t infer a particular doubling time just from the fact that the company has superintelligence. That depends on how quickly intelligence can translate into physical production.

r001.rationale: The response identifies factories, chips, motors, batteries, and electricity as physical constraints, but does not compare them with the challenge of learning to operate robots.

r002.rationale: It mentions using existing infrastructure and automating production, but does not propose converting car factories into robot factories.

r003.rationale: It describes deploying robots to make more robots and more factories, with output reinvested to expand the robot economy.

r004.rationale: It does not describe real-time coaching by superintelligence or unskilled workers performing construction tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d expect it to happen in stages. Having superintelligence doesn’t immediately give you a billion robots. You still need factories, materials, energy, and time to build things. But it could make the process of expanding that industrial capacity much faster.

Initially, the company could use human workers and existing suppliers to manufacture robots and build factories. The AI would do the engineering, coordinate production, and figure out where the bottlenecks are. As the robots become sufficiently capable and cheap, they could take over more of that work, including building the next generation of factories and robots.

Then you have this feedback loop: more robots let you build more manufacturing capacity, which lets you produce more robots. The important question is how quickly that loop can run. If you’re continually waiting for a particular chip factory or a new power plant, that could slow things down a lot. So I wouldn’t assume that intelligence alone makes the physical economy grow arbitrarily fast. But I do think it could enable growth much faster than we’re accustomed to, once enough of the production process is automated.

r001.rationale: The response says factories, materials, energy, and time constrain expansion, but does not compare physical robot production with superintelligence learning to operate robots.

r002.rationale: It mentions using existing suppliers and building factories, but does not propose converting car factories into robot factories.

r003.rationale: It describes a feedback loop in which robots build more manufacturing capacity and factories, enabling production of more robots.

r004.rationale: It says AI would coordinate production and help human workers, but does not describe real-time, step-by-step coaching that lets unskilled workers do construction.
